memoryText: Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God.
readingInstruction: No new reading today. Read Psalm 20:7 slowly, several times, and then say it from memory. Read the meditation and the week in review, and choose one of the three questions to write about, pray over, or share with someone.
memoryVerseMeditation:
This verse sets two kinds of trust side by side. It is a simple contrast, but it asks a searching question: where does your confidence rest?

Chariots and horses were the strongest military technology of the ancient Near East. An army with them was thought to be unbeatable. Israel was told not to depend on them (Deuteronomy 17:16; Isaiah 31:1). The psalm does not say that chariots are useless. It says that the people of God have a different foundation.

What are our chariots and horses? They are whatever we lean on for security instead of God. For some it is a bank account. For others, it is a résumé, a network of influential friends, good health, a clever plan, or a disciplined routine. These things are not evil. They are gifts. But when we trust in them, they become idols, and they fail.

“We trust in the name of the LORD our God.” In the Bible, a name stands for the whole person. To trust in God’s name is to trust in who he is: faithful, powerful, merciful, covenant-keeping. And notice the “we.” This is a community statement. We say it together, as a church.

The contrast in the next verse is vivid: “They collapse and fall, but we rise and stand upright.” Those who trust in horses fall. Those who trust in God stand.

For the Christian, the name of the LORD has been revealed in Jesus. “There is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved” (Acts 4:12). Hold this verse when you are tempted to feel safe because of something other than him.
weekInReview: This week you followed the end of Saul and the rise of David. You read Saul’s last night, when God was silent and he turned to a medium, and David’s response in his own low moment: he strengthened himself in the LORD his God. You read David’s lament over Saul and Jonathan, and how he became king first over Judah and then over all Israel. You saw him take Jerusalem and bring the ark to the city, after the sobering lesson of Uzzah. In the Psalms, you prayed for the king in Psalm 20 and gave thanks for him in Psalm 21. The week taught that God’s anointed trusts in the name of the LORD, that God’s holiness must be honored, and that true worship joins reverence with joy.
reflectionQuestions: David strengthened himself in the LORD when everything was taken from him. What does that look like for you in a hard season?
Psalm 21 says the king trusts in the LORD and will not be moved. How does Jesus, the King who trusted perfectly, give you security when you feel shaken?
What are the “chariots and horses” you are most tempted to trust? What would it look like to trust in the name of the LORD instead?
prayerPrompts: Thank God that you trust in his name and not in chariots.
Thank him for the King who trusts him perfectly.
